title: Bad Shepherds, a Righteous Branch, and False Prophets
summary: The LORD condemns the shepherds, Judah's kings and leaders, who scattered his flock, and promises to gather the remnant himself and raise up for David a righteous Branch called “The LORD Our Righteousness.” The rest of the chapter is a long indictment of the prophets of Jerusalem, who promise peace to the unrepentant, speak dreams of their own making, and have never stood in the LORD's council. It ends with a sharp play on the word “burden.”
story: Chapters 21 and 22 walked through the last kings of Judah one by one (Shallum, Jehoiakim, Coniah) and found each of them wanting. Chapter 23 draws the line under that series. If the house of David has failed as shepherd, God will shepherd his people himself and then give them a true king from David's line. Having dealt with kings, Jeremiah turns to the other institution that should have guarded the nation: the prophets. The court prophets of his day are the voices he contends with through the rest of the book, most memorably Hananiah in chapter 28. The chapter therefore sets up two questions that run through Jeremiah's middle chapters: who will rule God's people rightly, and how can anyone tell a true word from a false one?
historical:
The oracles in this chapter belong to the final decades of the kingdom of Judah, before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. The last king was Zedekiah, placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon in 597 BC after King Jehoiachin (called Coniah in 22:24) was taken into exile. Zedekiah's Hebrew name means roughly that the LORD is my righteousness. Most interpreters hear the royal name in verse 6, “The LORD Our Righteousness,” as a deliberate reversal: the coming king will truly be what Zedekiah's name only claimed.

The prophets in view were real public figures, often attached to the temple and the royal court, who reassured the nation that Babylon would not prevail and that Jerusalem, as the LORD's city, was safe. Verse 13 looks back to the northern kingdom, whose capital Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC; its prophets had spoken in the name of Baal, the Canaanite storm god. Jeremiah's point is that Jerusalem's prophets, who use the LORD's name, are worse.
cultural:
Across the ancient Near East, kings called themselves shepherds of their people; the image of a ruler as shepherd appears in royal inscriptions from Mesopotamia long before Jeremiah, and David himself had been a shepherd boy. So “shepherds” in verses 1 to 4 means rulers, not pastors in the modern sense. A good shepherd kept the flock together, found the lost, and protected it from predators. The charge here is that Judah's rulers did the opposite: they scattered the flock, which is to say their policies led to deportation and ruin.

Prophecy was an ordinary institution in Israel and its neighbors, and kings consulted prophets before battles. Israel believed a true prophet had “stood in the council of the LORD” (verse 18), the heavenly assembly around God's throne, like Micaiah's vision in 1 Kings 22. Dreams were a widely accepted means of divine revelation, which is why the false prophets could claim them. Jeremiah doesn't reject dreams as such; he rejects dreams that replace or contradict the word God has already spoken.
literary: The chapter has two large blocks. Verses 1 to 8 are a compact oracle of woe and hope, built on the verb “attend to” (Hebrew paqad): the shepherds have not attended to the flock, so the LORD will attend to them (verse 2). Verses 7 and 8 promise a new exodus so great that people will swear by it instead of by the exodus from Egypt; the same words appear in 16:14-15. Verses 9 to 40 were probably a separate collection headed “As for the prophets.” It opens with Jeremiah's own anguish (verse 9), moves through a series of charges and rhetorical questions, and piles up the refrain “I am against the prophets” three times (verses 30 to 32). The closing section (verses 33 to 40) turns on a pun: the Hebrew massa means both an “oracle” and a heavy “burden,” so when people ask for the burden of the LORD, the answer is that they are the burden, and he will cast them off.

outline.t: Woe to the shepherds; the LORD will gather his flock
The righteous Branch: The LORD Our Righteousness
A new exodus greater than the first
Jeremiah's grief over godless prophets and priests
They were never in the LORD's council
Dreams versus the word: straw and grain, fire and hammer
No more talk of the burden of the LORD

doctrines.note: Verses 5 and 6 are one of the Old Testament's clearest promises of a coming king from David's line who will do what the historical kings failed to do: rule wisely and administer justice and righteousness. The promise is repeated almost word for word in 33:15-16.

The chapter draws a line between God's word and human religious talk that borrows his name. A true word comes from the LORD's council, calls people to turn from evil (verse 22), and has the weight of grain and the force of fire and a hammer (verses 28-29). Comforting words that leave sin untouched are, by this test, suspect.

Verses 23 and 24 insist that the LORD is not a local deity who can be managed or hidden from. He is near and far at once, and he fills heaven and earth. False prophecy assumes a small God who will not notice.

words.note: Tsemach, branch or sprout, literally something that springs up from the ground. Used here for a new shoot from David's line, it became a title for the coming king in 33:15 and in Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12. The image fits a family tree that looked cut down by exile.

Sod, council or confidential counsel. It names the circle of trusted advisers who hear a king's plans, and here the heavenly assembly where the LORD's purposes are made known. A prophet's authority depended on having stood there (verses 18 and 22).

Massa, oracle. The word comes from the verb to lift or carry, so it also means a load or burden. Jeremiah plays on both senses in verses 33 to 40: the people who mockingly ask for the LORD's burden are told that they themselves have become the burden.

Paqad, to attend to, visit, or reckon with. The verb can mean caring for someone or calling them to account. Verse 2 uses both senses side by side: the shepherds did not attend to the flock, so the LORD will attend to them in judgment.

christ: The New Testament picks up both halves of verses 1 to 6. Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep and gathers them into one flock (John 10:11-16), standing where Jeremiah said the LORD himself would stand. Matthew describes Jesus looking on the crowds with compassion because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Matthew 9:36). Christians have read the righteous Branch of David, whose name is “The LORD Our Righteousness,” as fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David whom Paul says became for us righteousness from God (1 Corinthians 1:30). That link is a Christian reading of a royal promise rather than a direct quotation of this verse in the New Testament, but the promise of a Davidic king who would do justice is one the Gospels plainly claim Jesus fulfills. The warnings about prophets who promise peace without repentance also echo in Jesus' warnings about false prophets known by their fruit (Matthew 7:15-20).

hard.q: If both true and false prophets said “the LORD declares,” how was anyone supposed to tell the difference?
hard.a: It was genuinely hard, which is why the book spends so much time on it. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 offers one test, whether the word comes to pass, but that could only be applied afterward. Jeremiah adds tests that could be applied in the moment. A true prophet stands in the LORD's council and so speaks in line with what God has already revealed in his covenant; the false prophets promise peace to people who despise the LORD (verse 17). A true word calls people to turn from their evil ways (verse 22), while the false one strengthens the hands of evildoers (verse 14). The moral character of the prophet matters too: verse 14 charges them with adultery and lies. None of this made the choice easy for people living through it, and chapter 28 shows two prophets facing each other in the temple with opposite messages. But the chapter's criteria are not arbitrary: agreement with God's revealed character and a call to repentance are still sensible tests of any religious voice.

questions: Verse 17 describes preachers telling people who despise God that all will be well. What makes a message of peace true or false?
Why do you think Jeremiah's grief in verse 9 comes before his charges against the prophets? What difference does it make when a rebuke comes from someone who is heartbroken?
The chapter compares God's word to grain, fire, and a hammer. Which of those images describes your experience of Scripture, and which would you rather avoid?
